title: Teaching Portfolio
text:
My primary goal as an instructor is to make sure every student feels safe, welcome, and respected, and knows they belong in the mathematics classroom. Students arrive with very different experiences of mathematics, and some have had far more support and encouragement than others. I share the conviction behind Federico Ardila-Mantilla’s axioms for mathematics education that mathematical talent is distributed equally across groups of people, and every student deserves meaningful mathematical experiences and to be treated with dignity and respect.
Below are some aspects of my teaching philosophy, and how they show up in the courses I have taught. My full teaching statement (PDF) has more detail.

title: Teaching Portfolio
text:
Teaching philosophy

In the classroom

Doing mathematics, not just watching it. After introducing a concept and working an example, I give students time to try a related problem before I present a solution. I walk around the room, offering small hints and asking questions that help them find a next step.
Mistakes are part of the work. When a student is unsure or makes a mistake, my first concern is to help them feel at ease. An incomplete idea is still worth discussing, and I openly acknowledge my own mistakes.
Finding the right picture. A good picture often makes sense before a formal statement does. In MTH 314 I used geometric transformations of the plane so that students understood what eigenvalues and eigenvectors tell us about a linear transformation while they learned to compute them.
Asking why, not just how. My MTH 317H worksheets ask why a concept is useful or needed, not only how to apply it.



Learning together
Explaining an idea to a classmate is one of the best ways to understand it, and asking a classmate is often easier than asking the instructor. In person, I build group work into class time. Online, where students rarely get to meet their peers, I design the course so that live sessions are spent working on problems together.


Caring for the whole student

Flexibility. My students have lives and pressures outside my course. When a student faces difficult circumstances, I offer flexible deadlines so they can complete the work rather than fall behind for reasons beyond their control.
A fair chance to prepare. I space exams so students have time to prepare, and I avoid scheduling one right after a long weekend or break.
Reaching out. In an online course a struggling student can easily go unnoticed. I write to students who are not doing well and meet with them individually.
Another chance to show mastery. With standards-based grading, an unsuccessful attempt becomes a reason to keep working rather than a final verdict.



Feedback
I check understanding with short exit tickets and low-stakes worksheets, and I release complete solutions after each deadline so students can check their own reasoning. I also keep listening to what students tell me about their learning, and adjust.


Technology, including AI
I use technology where it serves learning: live writing on an iPad projected to every table, recorded videos, Zoom options for bad-weather days, and Python assignments for the computational side of linear algebra.
Generative AI makes it more important to design activities that reveal how students think. Where course policies permit, I would invite students to critique an AI-generated solution: find the unsupported steps and explain how to fix them. They might also use AI to suggest examples to investigate, while checking every claim against course materials. I would make expectations for acknowledging AI help explicit and offer equivalent activities that do not need AI. Written reasoning, discussion, and reflection would remain at the center of how I assess understanding.

title: Teaching Portfolio
text:
Teaching in different settings
MTH 103A: College Algebra I (instructor, Spring 2025). About sixty students in an active-learning classroom in the MSU Union, with round tables and screens throughout the room. Students worked in groups while two undergraduate learning assistants and I moved between tables. The class met daily at 8 a.m. through a Michigan winter, so I offered a Zoom option for icy mornings and possible closures. I wrote my own notes and worksheets and used standards-based grading.
MTH 124: Survey of Calculus (instructor, Summer 2023, online). I ran the course as a flipped classroom: students watched videos I recorded before class, so our live sessions could be spent working through problems and discussing solutions together. The course used Piazza for questions, and students could optionally record a short video introducing themselves to help them find classmates to work with.
MTH 314: Matrix Algebra with Applications (instructor, Summer 2024, online). I wrote lecture notes in LaTeX and also shared the handwritten notes from each Zoom lecture, so students had both a polished reference and a record of how each argument unfolded. I recorded lecture videos and short check-ins between meetings, and designed in-class Python assignments.
MTH 317H: Honors Linear Algebra (recitation leader, Fall 2026). I teach the proof techniques from MTH 299 that students need but may not yet know. The notes and worksheets are on the course page.

Projects

Arithmetic statistics of p-torsion in class groups of quartic number fields
2026–present · Arithmetic Geometry at UNT 2, University of North Texas · Sameera Vemulapalli’s project group · Repository
We study p-torsion in class groups of quartic number fields that admit an integral basis of the form 1, x, y, xy, in connection with Bhargava’s parametrizations of quartic rings. The repository has some Magma code and preliminary analysis.


Efficient computation of the Weil pairing for Drinfeld modules
2026–present · Rethinking Number Theory (online, June 22–July 3, 2026) · Antoine Leudière’s project group
We’re working toward explicit computation of Weil pairings for Drinfeld modules by implementing pairing algorithms in SageMath and other open-source software.


Who bears the congestion price?
Summer 2026 · Erdős Institute Data Science Boot Camp · Repository
On January 5, 2025, New York became the first US city to charge vehicles for entering a defined zone: the Manhattan Central Business District south of 60th Street. Using public TLC trip records (about 37M Yellow taxi trips and about 202M Uber/Lyft trips, February–June 2024 compared with the same months of 2025), we ask who bears this fee and whether it reduced trips.

The burden is uneven, and the finding is stable. A flat per-trip fee is a much larger share of short, low-cost trips, which are concentrated in the dense Manhattan core, than of long airport trips. The zone ranking stays stable across the tested denominator floors, giving a reusable, reproducible burden metric (DS_z).
The volume models show suggestive negative patterns. Three regression-with-controls designs compare burden, exposure, and vehicle groups. A 2023→2024 no-fee placebo and sensitivity checks limit a direct fee-caused interpretation.

I am a fifth-year Ph.D. candidate in mathematics at Michigan State University, working with Prof. Georgios Pappas. I completed a B.S.–M.S. dual degree in mathematics at IISER Tirupati in 2022, where I worked with Prof. D. S. Nagaraj and wrote my master’s thesis on class field theory.
I am broadly interested in arithmetic geometry and representation theory, specifically finite group actions on algebraic varieties and the Galois module structure of their cohomology groups. Recently I have been working on Deligne–Lusztig varieties; see my preprint under preparation and the research page.
Outside mathematics, I enjoy Carnatic and Hindustani classical music, playing the bansuri (Indian bamboo flute), badminton, literature, and social justice advocacy.

title: Galois module structure of Deligne–Lusztig varieties for \mathbf{G} = \mathrm{GL}_3

title: Galois module structure of Deligne–Lusztig varieties for \mathbf{G} = \mathrm{GL}_3
text:
Summary
Deligne and Lusztig defined a finite étale cover Y(w) \to X(w) of varieties. It is attached to any connected reductive group \mathbf{G} defined over a finite field \mathbb{F}_q, with a Frobenius endomorphism F, and to a Weyl group element w \in W.
We consider the ramified Galois covers 
\overline{Y(w)} \longrightarrow \overline{X(w)}
 of the natural compactifications of these Deligne–Lusztig varieties. Our goal is to calculate the Lefschetz numbers for the action of the covering group on the coherent cohomology of the structure sheaf of \overline{Y(w)}. The covering group is \mathbf{T}^{wF}, the \mathbb{F}_p-points of a torus.
These numbers determine the representation of \mathbf{T}^{wF} on the alternating sum 
\sum_i (-1)^i \, H^i\big(\overline{Y(w)}, \mathcal{O}_{\overline{Y(w)}}\big).
 The paper gives these Lefschetz numbers explicitly for Deligne–Lusztig surfaces, in the cases \mathbf{G}^F = \mathrm{GL}_3(\mathbb{F}_p) and \mathbf{G}^F = \mathrm{U}_3(\mathbb{F}_p).

title: Galois module structure of Deligne–Lusztig varieties for \mathbf{G} = \mathrm{GL}_3
text:
Method
The approach is to work étale-locally to resolve the singularities of \overline{Y(w)}, and to construct a smooth model carrying an action of \mathbf{T}^{wF} that extends the action on \overline{Y(w)}. The local calculations lead to toric geometry. The Hirzebruch–Jung algorithm for minimal resolutions of toric surfaces then supplies what is needed to apply the Lefschetz–Riemann–Roch theorem. In both the split and the unitary case, the resulting Lefschetz numbers are explicit and nonzero.

title: Galois module structure of Deligne–Lusztig varieties for \mathbf{G} = \mathrm{GL}_3
text:
Background: geometric Galois module theory
Geometric Galois module theory studies how a finite group acting on an algebraic variety or scheme gives module structures on its cohomological and arithmetic invariants. If a finite group G acts on a variety X, then G acts naturally on cohomology groups such as H^i(X, \mathcal{F}). These groups can then be studied as modules over the group ring k[G], or over the corresponding integral group rings in arithmetic settings.
A central problem is to determine these module structures, and their equivariant Euler characteristics, for a Galois cover X \to X/G. This extends classical Galois module theory to higher dimensions. In the classical theory, one studies rings of integers in finite Galois extensions of local or global fields as modules over group rings.
The subject draws on arithmetic geometry, algebraic geometry, representation theory, and algebraic K-theory. Ramification and fixed-point data play a central role in the structure of the resulting Galois modules.

title: MTH 317H: Honors Linear Algebra
text:
MTH 317H is an advanced introduction to linear algebra and abstract vector spaces, with a strong emphasis on mathematical communication. Students learn to construct logical arguments and write clear, rigorous proofs.
The course has two lecture sections that meet on Tuesdays and Thursdays and cover the linear algebra. I lead the Monday recitations. For roughly the first half of the semester, recitation is an accelerated introduction to proof writing (essentially the content of MTH 299), taught through notes and collaborative worksheets. Later recitations practice the linear algebra from lecture. Most recitations begin with a 10-minute quiz.
Learning objectives

Understand and use key concepts of linear algebra: vector spaces, linear transformations, systems of linear equations, determinants, and eigenvalues and eigenvectors.
Gain proficiency in constructing and writing proofs.

Texts (all free online, except the last two)

Sheldon Axler, Linear Algebra Done Right, 4th ed. (LADR)
Sergei Treil, Linear Algebra Done Wrong (LADW)
Richard Hammack, Book of Proof, 3rd ed.
Kevin Houston, How to Think Like a Mathematician
Chartrand, Polimeni and Zhang, Mathematical Proofs: A Transition to Advanced Mathematics
